'''''Symphytum officinale''''' is a [[perennial]] [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Boraginaceae]]. Along with 34 other species of ''Symphytum'', it is known as '''comfrey''' (from the Latin {{Lang|la|confervere}} to 'heal' or literally to 'boil together', referring to uses in ancient [[traditional medicine]]). Internal or long-term [[topical medication|topical]] use of comfrey is discouraged due to its strong potential to cause [[hepatotoxicity|liver toxicity]].<ref name="drugs"/>

To differentiate it from other members of the genus ''Symphytum'', this species is known as '''common comfrey'''<ref name="NPDT"/> or '''true comfrey'''. Other English names include '''boneset''', '''knitbone''', '''consound''', and '''slippery-root'''.<ref name="grin"/> 

It is native to Europe, growing in damp, grassy places. It is found throughout Ireland and Britain on river banks and ditches. It occurs in North America as an [[introduced species]] and [[weed]]. The flowers are mostly visited by [[bumblebee]]s.<ref name="vdKooi2015"/>

==History==
Over centuries, comfrey was cultivated in Asia, and Europe including the United Kingdom as a vegetable and [[herbalism|herbal medicine]].<ref name="drugs"/><ref name="ema"/><ref name="pf"/> Its early common names, ''knitbone'' or ''boneset'', reflect its historical use by [[poultice]]s of leaves and roots to treat sprains, bruises or bone fractures.<ref name="drugs"/><ref name="ema"/> The roots were mashed then packed around a broken limb, and once dried they formed a hardened 'plaster cast'.<ref name="Readers"/>

==Description==
The plant can grow {{convert|1-5|ft|m|1|order=flip}} tall<ref name="Poland2009"/> with branched, strongly winged stems. The root system has a pronounced [[taproot]], reaching up to 1.8 m deep.<ref name="Oberdorfer2001" /> The internally white roots are covered with black bark. Above ground the plant is covered in long, downward-pointing, tapering hairs that are bristly on the stems and softer on the leaves. Along the erect stems grow large simple, mostly stalked leaves in an alternate pattern. They are oval-lanceolate and {{Convert|4 to 25|cm|frac=2}} long. In the upper parts they are narrower, without stalks, and with margins that extend down the stems. The [[chromosome count]] is 2n = 24, 26, 36, 40, 48 or 54.<ref name="Oberdorfer2001"/>

===Inflorescence and fruit===
The plant flowers from May to June with forked [[Inflorescence#Determinate or cymose|cymes]] that are initially coiled and later open out.<ref name="Readers"/> They bear two rows of hermaphrodite flowers on nodding stalks that are {{Convert|2 to 6|mm|frac=16}} long.<ref name="FloraWeb"/> The small flowers measure {{Convert|8–20|mm|abbr=on|frac=4}} in length and 12 to 18 mm across the corolla. The flowers are radially symmetrical with five equal petals that are fused into a tubular or narrowly bell-shaped corolla with pointed, recurved teeth that are 2 mm long. Petals come in mainly two colours – typically cream to yellow or pink to purplish. Inside are 5 stamens and 1 stigma. The calyx has a tubular segment of about 2 mm and narrow, pointed teeth of about 4 mm. The fruits are segmented into 4 egg-shaped, shiny black nutlets that are 5–6 mm long. The plant produces significant nectar when compared to other UK plants tested.<ref name="Pollinators"/> Although, it has a long tube, meaning only insects with long tongues can reach the nectar, some bees have been known to bite into the side of the flower to access the nectar – a foraging behaviour known as [[nectar robbing]].<ref name="Readers"/>

===Species differentiation===
[[File:Common comfrey in port edward.webp|thumb|[[Decurrent]] leaf bases of common comfrey]]
With ''Symphytum'' × ''uplandicum'', leaf bases are not decurrent, stem internodes are not winged, and the surfaces of the seeds are brown, dull, and finely granular instead of shiny black.<ref name="Jepson" /> Additionally, ''S.'' × ''uplandicum'' is generally more bristly, flowers later (between June and August),<ref name="Readers"/> and its flowers tend to be more blue or violet.<ref name="Stace2010"/>

==Taxonomy==
The latin name epithet ''[[officinalis|officinale]]'' refers to its use for medicinal preparations. The official first formal scientific [[species description]] appeared in 1753 in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]], Tomus I, page 136.<ref name="Tropicos"/>

Subspecies include subsp. ''uliginosum'' (A. Kern.) Nyman (syn. ''S. uliginosum'' auct. non Kern., ''S. tanaicense''), subsp. ''officinale'', and subsp. ''bohemicum'' (F. W. Schmidt) Čelak (syn. ''S. bohemicum'').

A common hybrid is formed between ''Symphytum officinale'' and ''[[Symphytum asperum|S. asperum]]'', [[Symphytum × uplandicum|''Symphytum'' × ''uplandicum'']], also known as Blue Comfrey,<ref name="Readers"/> or Russian comfrey, which is widespread in the British Isles, interbreeds with ''S. officinale'', and represents the economically most important kind of comfrey.<ref name="Hills2011"/>

== Distribution and habitat ==
Comfrey is found in moist grasslands or along riverbanks and ditches in western Asia, Europe, and North America.<ref name="pf" /> It is a [[perennial]] herb that is [[cold hardy]] down to {{convert|−35|C|F}} and [[drought tolerant]].

== Toxicity ==
Comfrey is mildly toxic. Like most Boraginaceae, it contains [[pyrrolizidine alkaloid]]s which are toxic compounds readily absorbed via the stomach or skin, and have potential to increase the risk of fatal liver toxicity.<ref name="drugs" /><ref name="ema" /><ref name="Oberlies2007" /> In 2001, the US [[Food and Drug Administration]] and [[Federal Trade Commission]] banned the sale of comfrey products for internal use and use on open wounds due to its potential toxicities.<ref name="fda2001" /><ref name="ftc" /> A 2018 review on pyrrolizidine alkaloids present in comfrey indicated widespread potential toxicity to humans and [[livestock]], and the opportunity for [[drug development]] from these compounds.<ref name="Moreira" />

== Uses ==
Despite its toxicity, the leaves and shoots have been considered edible, even raw; the stalks are said to be best collected prior to flowering and [[Blanching (cooking)|blanched]] prior to steaming; the leaves may also be used in tea.<ref name="tfb">{{Cite book |last=Francis-Baker |first=Tiffany |title=Concise Foraging Guide |date=2021 |publisher=[[Bloomsbury Publishing|Bloomsbury]] |isbn=978-1-4729-8474-6 |series=[[The Wildlife Trusts]] |location=London |page=77}}</ref>

=== Traditional medicine ===
In [[folklore]], ''Symphytum officinale'' roots were used in [[traditional medicine]] internally (as a [[herbal tea]] or tincture) or externally (as ointment, compresses, or alcoholic [[extract]]) for treatment of various disorders.<ref name="drugs"/><ref name="pf"/><ref name="Vogl2013"/> [[John Gerard]], an English herbalist (1545–1612), mentions "the slimie substance of the roote made in a [[possett]] of ale" would help back pains.{{cn|date=February 2024}} [[Poultice]]s may be used with the intent to heal broken bones, giving it the name "knitbone".<ref name="drugs"/> For such topical uses, comfrey can be infused in oil to then be mixed into ointments or balms.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Dadachanji |first1=Amaia |title=Wild Apothecary: Reclaiming Plant Medicine for All |date=2021 |publisher=Aeon Books Limited |location=London |isbn=978-1912807239 |edition=1st}}</ref> 

In 2004, a double-blind, randomized study of patients suffering from acute ankle sprains found that comfrey's anti-inflammatory and analgesic properties to be highly effective, in addition to its tissue regenerating abilities. No adverse reactions were observed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Koll |first1=R |last2=Buhr |first2=M |last3=Dieter |first3=R |last4=Pabst |first4=H |last5=Predel |first5=HG |last6=Petrowicz |first6=O |last7=Giannetti |first7=B |last8=Klingenburg |first8=S |last9=Staiger |first9=C |title=Efficacy and tolerance of a comfrey root extract (Extr. Rad. Symphyti) in the treatment of ankle distorsions: results of a multicenter, randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study. |journal=Phytomedicine |date=September 2004 |volume=11 |issue=6 |pages=470–7 |doi=10.1016/j.phymed.2004.02.001 |pmid=15500257}}</ref>

A 2013 review of clinical studies assessing the possible effect of comfrey on [[osteoarthritis]] found the research quality was too low to allow conclusions about its efficacy and safety.<ref name="cameron"/> In Europe as of 2015, there were no comfrey products for oral use, and those for topical uses to treat bruises or joint pain were evaluated as having risk of liver toxicity.<ref name="ema"/>
